Surah 64, verses 1–4, from al-Zamakhshari's commentary (*al-Kashshaf*):

Its status is disputed. It has eighteen verses [revealed after Surat al-Tahrim].

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The two adverbial phrases are placed first to indicate that dominion and praise belong exclusively to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is because dominion in the true sense belongs to Him, since He is the origin and originator of everything, the one who sustains it and the one who watches over it. Likewise praise belongs to Him, since the roots and branches of all blessings come from Him. As for the dominion of others, it is a delegation and a trust granted by Him, and their praise is an acknowledgment that Allah's blessing has passed through their hands.

﴿It is He who created you; among you is the disbeliever and among you is the believer﴾. That is: among you is one who brings about disbelief and performs it [[His statement "among you is one who brings about disbelief and performs it" interprets the verse according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school): that the servant is the creator of his voluntary actions. The doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah (the orthodox majority) is that the servant has no part in his action except acquisition (kasb), and its real creator is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as evidenced by His statement ﴿And Allah created you and what you do﴾. Just as the creation of the disbeliever does not necessitate blame, as he will state, so the creation of his disbelief does not necessitate blame, because it is for a wisdom, even if it is hidden from us. (ʿ)]] and among you is one who brings about belief [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning: among you is one who brings about disbelief and performs it, and among you is one who brings about belief..." etc. Ahmad said: He has mounted a blind camel and stumbled like a stumbling she-camel. He has plunged into a rough path where the traveler is ruined and the one who passes through it falls. He is only leading toward the pits of the arak tree, and circling around the pastures of polytheism. He digs but only to his own death with his hoof, and he pretends to be clever when he is only boasting. He claims to have certainty when he is only transgressing. Suppose he turned away from the rational proofs and the transmitted texts that are unanimous that Allah is the Creator of everything, and suppose what he claims about the visible world were consistent. But among his principles is analogizing the unseen to the seen, and he has resorted to acknowledging that Allah is the creator of the servant who performs the ugly act, and that creating the servant who performs the ugly act is like giving a sharp sword to a wicked man, and that this is ugly in the visible realm. It does not follow that the same is ugly in the creation of Allah, the Exalted. Could it not be that it contains a wisdom which Allah has kept to Himself? What guarantees him against the claim that the actions of the servant, even if rational people find them ugly, are created by Allah, and that in their creation there is a wisdom which Allah has kept to Himself? Is the difference then anything but sheer arbitrariness and the following of desire? Moreover, before he could master these principles, it would have to be possible to pull the thorn bush out of its thorns, or for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle.]] and performs it, as in His statement ﴿We placed in their offspring prophethood and the Scripture; so among them is one who is guided, and many of them are defiant﴾. The evidence for this is His statement ﴿And Allah is Seer of what you do﴾, that is, Knower of your disbelief and your belief, which are both among your deeds. The meaning is: He is the One who bestowed upon you the foundation of blessings, which is creation and bringing into existence from nothing. It was therefore obligatory for you to look with correct insight and to be, all of you, grateful servants. Yet you did not do so, despite your capacity, but rather you split into factions and divided into nations. Thus among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer. Disbelief is mentioned first because it is the predominant and most numerous among them. It has been said: He is the One who created you, so among you is a disbeliever in the creation, namely the Dahriyyah (materialists who deny a Creator), and among you is a believer in it.

If you say: Indeed, the servants are the ones who perform disbelief, but it was already known in the knowledge of the All-Wise that if He created them they would not commit anything but disbelief, and would not choose anything else. Then what prompted Him to create them, knowing what would come from them? And is the creator of the ugly act not one and the same as the creator of the one who performs it? Is this not like one who gives a sharp sword to a man known for cutting the road and killing a sacred soul, and he then kills a believer with it? Do not rational people agree on blaming and rebuking the giver, and striking his scalp [[His statement "striking his scalp": in al-Sihah, al-faruwah is the skin of the head. Al-faruwah also means a dry clump of gathered vegetation. (ʿ)]] just as they blame the killer? Rather, their reproach of the giver is even more severe.

I say: We know that Allah is All-Wise, Knowing of the ugliness of the ugly, and free of need of it. We know that all His acts are good, and that the creation of the doer of the ugly act is His act, and therefore it must be good and must have a good aspect to it. The hiddenness of the good aspect from us does not detract from its goodness, just as our ignorance of the wisdom behind the creation of most of His creatures does not detract from their goodness. ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾, with a right purpose and a profound wisdom, which is that He made them dwelling places for the responsible beings so that they might act, and He would then recompense them. ﴿And He shaped you and perfected your forms﴾. It is read "ṣawwarakum" with a kasra [ṣawwarakum, so that you may give thanks]. ﴿And to Him is the final return﴾, so your recompense will be for gratitude and for neglecting it.

If you say: How did He perfect their forms? I say: He made them the most beautiful and the most splendid of all living beings, as proof that a human does not wish that his form were other than what he sees of the other forms. And among the beauty of his form is that he was created upright, not hunched, as the Mighty and Majestic said ﴿in the best stature﴾.

If you say: How many ugly, deformed, and repulsive-looking people are there whom eyes recoil from? I say: There is no ugliness at all. Rather, beauty, like other qualities, has levels and ranks. The fact that some forms fall far below the ranks of those above them, and their comparison with those surpassing them, makes them unpleasing. Otherwise they are included within the domain of beauty and do not lie outside its boundary. Do you not see that you may admire a form and find it pleasing, though it is not your ideal, and then see something more graceful and higher in the ranks of beauty, so that your gaze turns away from the first, and you find it burdensome to look at after you were captivated by it and infatuated with it? The wise have said: Two things have no limit: beauty and eloquence.

He drew attention, through His knowledge, to what is in the heavens and the earth, then through His knowledge to what the servants conceal and what they make public, then through His knowledge to the contents of the breasts, to the effect that nothing of the universals or the particulars is hidden from Him or escapes Him. It is therefore fitting that He be feared and guarded against, and that one not dare to do anything that opposes His pleasure. The repetition of knowledge carries the meaning of repeated warning. Everything He mentions after His statement ﴿among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ is, as you see, in the sense of a warning against disbelief, and a denunciation of disobeying the Creator and failing to thank His blessing. How ignorant is the one who mixes disbelief with creation [[His statement "how ignorant is the one who mixes disbelief with creation": he means the Ahl al-Sunnah, who say that He, the Exalted, is the Creator of the actions of the servants, including disbelief and other sins. There is no basis for calling them ignorant, given that they rely on His statement ﴿And Allah created you and what you do﴾. (ʿ)]] and includes it among its components! Creation is the greatest blessing of Allah upon His servants, and disbelief is the greatest ingratitude of the servants toward their Lord.

He drew attention, through His knowledge, to what is in the heavens and the earth, then through His knowledge to what the servants conceal and what they make public, then through His knowledge to the contents of the breasts, to the effect that nothing of the universals or the particulars is hidden from Him or escapes Him. It is therefore fitting that He be feared and guarded against, and that one not dare to do anything that opposes His pleasure. The repetition of knowledge carries the meaning of repeated warning. Everything He mentions after His statement ﴿among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ is, as you see, in the sense of a warning against disbelief, and a denunciation of disobeying the Creator and failing to thank His blessing. How ignorant is the one who mixes disbelief with creation [[His statement "how ignorant is the one who mixes disbelief with creation": he means the Ahl al-Sunnah, who say that He, the Exalted, is the Creator of the actions of the servants, including disbelief and other sins. There is no basis for calling them ignorant, given that they rely on His statement ﴿And Allah created you and what you do﴾. (ʿ)]] and includes it among its components! Creation is the greatest blessing of Allah upon His servants, and disbelief is the greatest ingratitude of the servants toward their Lord.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 64, verses 5–6:

أَلَمْ يَأْتِكُمْ: The address is to the disbelievers of Makkah. Wa-dhalika (وذلِكَ) is a reference to what was mentioned of the calamity they tasted in this world and the punishment prepared for them in the Hereafter. Bi-annahu (بِأَنَّهُ): because the matter and the report is that "كانَتْ تَأْتِيهِمْ رُسُلُهُمْ" (their messengers used to come to them)...... "أَبَشَرٌ يَهْدُونَنا" (Shall mere humans guide us?). They denied that the messengers could be human, yet they did not deny that God could be a stone.

وَاسْتَغْنَى اللَّهُ (And God was self-sufficient): the word is unrestricted so that it encompasses everything, including their faith and obedience. If you say: the statement "وَتَوَلَّوْا وَاسْتَغْنَى اللَّهُ" (and they turned away, and God was self-sufficient) seems to imply that turning away and self-sufficiency exist together [[Mahmud said: "He left it unrestricted so that it encompasses everything; then he said: If you say, turning away was in them... etc." Ahmad said: The truth is that He did not create faith for them, nor the capacity for it, so He was able to create faith and the capacity for it for them. Al-Zamakhshari twisted it toward his own principle.]], whereas God, exalted is He, has always been self-sufficient. I say: its meaning is: the self-sufficiency of God became manifest in that He did not compel them to faith nor force them to it, although He was able to do so.

Al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 64, verses 7–8:

Al-zaʻm (claim): a claim to knowledge. From it is his (ﷺ) saying: "Zaʻamū is the steed of falsehood" [[I have not found it narrated as a marfuʻ report with this wording, though it has been mentioned earlier at the beginning of al-Baqarah with the wording "Evil is the steed of a man toward falsehood, zaʻamūh." It has also been mentioned from Shurayh: "Zaʻamū is the kunyah (euphemistic name) of falsehood."]]. And from Shurayh: everything has a kunyah, and the kunyah of falsehood is "zaʻamū." It transitively takes two objects, like the verb of knowing (ʻilm). He said:

"... and I did not think you would be spared from that"
[[And indeed he who lives, O Umm Malik ... will die, and I did not think you would be spared from that.

He means: indeed every living being, however long its life, will die, and I did not think you, O Umm Malik, would be spared from that judgment or death. Al-maʻzal is the place of seclusion and isolation; that is, I did not consider you to be in a place apart from it, or possessing a place apart from it, or one who isolates herself from it. Or the said statement itself, as an intensification.]]

And inna together with what is in its scope stands in place of the two objects. "Those who disbelieved" refers to the people of Makkah. "Balā" is an affirmation of what follows "lan," namely the resurrection. "And that is upon Allah easy" means nothing diverts Him from it. By "His Messenger and the light" he means Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an.

Qur'anic recitation variants: "نجمعكم" and "نكفر" and "وندخله" were also read with the yā' and nūn forms.

If you ask: by what is the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) "yawma" in the verse put in the accusative? I say: it is governed by His saying "latunabbu'unna" (you will surely be informed), or by "khabīr" (All-Aware), because of the sense of threat (wa'īd) in it, as if it were said: "And Allah will punish you on the day He gathers you." Or it is governed by an implied "udhkur" (remember): "the Day of Assembly," meaning, "the day on which the first and the last will be gathered."

At-taghābun (mutual deception in loss): it is a metaphor taken from people cheating one another in trade, where some of them defraud others. It refers to the happy (su'adā') descending into the places of the wretched (ashqiyā') which they would have occupied had they been happy, and the wretched descending into the places of the happy which they would have occupied had they been wretched. In this there is mockery of the wretched, since their descent is not a loss.

In a hadith of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "No servant enters Paradise except that he is shown his seat in the Fire, had he done evil, so that he increases in gratitude. And no servant enters the Fire except that he is shown his seat in Paradise, had he done good, so that he increases in regret." [Narrated by al-Bukhari from the narration of al-A'raj from Abu Hurayrah. In the agreed-upon (Muttafaq 'alayh) hadith from Anas, in the story of the believer, it is said to him: "Look at your seat in the Fire; Allah has replaced it for you with a seat in Paradise." The Prophet said: "He sees them both together." And in the report from Ibn 'Umar: "When any one of you dies, his seat is presented to him morning and evening," and so on.]

The meaning of "dhālika yawmu at-taghābun" (that is the Day of Mutual Deception), though people may deceive one another on other days, is to magnify that day, and that its deception is the true deception, not the deception in worldly matters, however great and grand they may be. "Ṣāliḥan" is an adjective of the verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: a righteous deed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 64, verse 11:

"By the permission of Allah" (إِلَّا بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ): i.e., by His decree and His will, as though He had given permission for the calamity to befall him. "He guides his heart" (يَهْدِ قَلْبَهُ): He shows him kindness and expands his breast to increase him in obedience and good. It was also said: it refers to saying "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return" (al-istirja') at the time of calamity. And from al-Dahhak: "He guides his heart until he knows that what befell him would not have missed him, and what missed him would not have befallen him."

And from Mujahid: "If he is tested, he is patient; if he is given, he is grateful; and if he is wronged, he forgives."

It has also been recited as yuhda qalbuhu (with the verb in the passive), and "the heart" (al-qalb) is then either in the nominative or the accusative. The reasoning for the accusative: it is like safiha nafsahu (he was foolish in himself), meaning: he is foolish in his heart. It is also possible that the meaning is: the disbeliever is lost from his heart and far from it, while the believer finds his heart and is guided to it, like His saying, Exalted is He: "Surely in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart" (لِمَنْ كانَ لَهُ قَلْبٌ). It has also been recited as nahdi qalbahu (with the nun). Yahdi qalbahu, meaning: yahtadi (he is guided). Yahda'u qalbuhu: yatma'inn (his heart is at rest).

Yahdi, and yahda' with the hamza softened (al-takhfif). "And Allah is All-Knowing of everything" (وَاللَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ): He knows what kindness affects among hearts and what it does not affect, so He grants it and withholds it.

Then if you turn away, there is nothing upon him (the Messenger) if you turn away, since it was not prescribed for him to compel your obedience; he was only prescribed to convey and make clear, and no more. ﴿And upon Allah let the believers put their trust﴾. This is an exhortation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to place his trust in Him and to rely upon Him in his affair, until He grants him victory over those who denied him and turned away from him.

Al-Zamakhshari, *al-Kashshaf*, commentary on Surah 64, verses 14–15:

Indeed, among your spouses there are some who are enemies to you, so beware of them (﴿فَاحْذَرُوهُمْ﴾). Among your children there are some who are enemies to their fathers, who disobey them and cause them grief and harm. The pronoun in ﴿فَاحْذَرُوهُمْ﴾ refers either to the enemy, or to spouses and children together. That is: since you know that these people are never free of an enemy, be on your guard against them, and do not feel secure against their harm and evil. ﴿وَإِنْ تَعْفُوا﴾, that is, if you pardon them when you discover enmity from them and do not respond to them in kind, then ﴿فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ يَغْفِرُ لَكُمْ﴾, God will forgive your sins and expiate them for you.

It has been said that some people intended to emigrate from Makkah, but their spouses and children discouraged them and said, "You are leaving and abandoning us." They felt pity for them and stayed behind. Later, when they did emigrate and saw that those who had preceded them had gained understanding of the religion, they wanted to punish their spouses and children, but forgiveness was made appealing to them.

It has also been said that they said to them, "Where are you going, abandoning your country, your kin and your wealth?" So they became angry with them and said, "If God gathers us in the land of emigration, we will not treat you well." When they emigrated, they withheld good from them, so they were urged to pardon them and to restore to them kindness and maintenance.

It has also been said that ʿAwf ibn Mālik al-Ashjaʿī had a family and children. Whenever he wished to go on a military campaign (ghazw), they clung to him, wept before him and softened his heart, so it seemed that he intended to harm them. Then this was revealed.

﴿فِتْنَةٌ﴾ means trial and affliction, because they lead one into sin and punishment, and there is no greater affliction than these. Do you not see His saying: ﴿وَاللَّهُ عِنْدَهُ أَجْرٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ (and God has a great reward with Him)?

In a hadith (prophetic report): "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: 'His dependents consumed his good deeds.'" [I have not seen it traced to the Prophet. Abū Nuʿaym narrated it in *al-Ḥilya*, in the biography of Sufyān al-Thawrī, as his own statement. ʿAlī ibn Maʿbad narrated in *al-Ṭāʿa wa-l-Maʿṣiya* from Isḥāq ibn Abī Yaḥyā, from ʿAbd al-Malik, from Bukayr, who said: "On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: 'Where are those whose dependents consumed their good deeds? Stand up, for the resurrection is before you.'"]

And from some of the early Muslims: "Dependents are the woodworm of acts of obedience."

And it is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was delivering a sermon when al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn came, wearing two red shirts, stumbling and getting up again. He came down to them, took them, placed them in his lap on the pulpit, and said: "God has spoken truly: ﴿إِنَّمَا أَمْوَالُكُمْ وَأَوْلَادُكُمْ فِتْنَةٌ﴾ (Your wealth and your children are only a trial). I saw these two boys and I could not be patient with them." Then he resumed his sermon. [Compilers of the Sunan collections, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Ibn Abī Shayba, Abū Yaʿlā and al-Bazzār narrated it through Ḥusayn ibn Wāqid, from Ibn Burayda, from his father. Al-Bazzār said: "We know of no route for it other than this one."]

It has also been said: if you are able to wage jihad and emigrate, then let the inclination toward wealth and children not tempt you away from them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 64, verse 16:

﴿مَا اسْتَطَعْتُمْ﴾ means with your utmost effort and your full capacity; that is, exert your ability in it. ﴿وَاسْمَعُوا﴾ means listen to what you are admonished with. ﴿وَأَطِيعُوا﴾ means obey in what you are commanded and in what you are forbidden. ﴿وَأَنْفِقُوا﴾ means spend in the channels in which spending has become obligatory upon you. ﴿خَيْراً لِأَنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a verb omitted from the sentence, its implied sense being: "Do good for your own souls" (ائتوا خيرا لأنفسكم), and do what is better and more beneficial for them. This is an emphasis on urging compliance with these commands, and a clarification that these matters are better for your souls than wealth, children, and what you are devoted to of the love of desires and the adornments of this world.

Zamakhshari's commentary on the Qur'an, al-Kashshaf, on surah 64, verses 17–18:

And mention of "the loan" (al-qard): a gentle way of soliciting. "He will multiply it for you" means He will record for you ten, or seven hundred, for each one, up to whatever increase He wills. It is also read "yuḍā'ifahu" (yuda'ifahu). "Shakūr" is figurative (majāz), meaning: He does with you what one who is extremely thankful does, namely great reward. Likewise "Ḥalīm" means He does with you what one who shows forbearance toward the wrongdoer does, so He does not hasten to punish you despite the abundance of your sins.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah at-Taghabun, sudden death will be lifted from him."

[The hadith was narrated by al-Tha'labi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wahidi with their chains of transmission going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him).]
